My first choir concert

Our school choir ____1____ (meet) every Tuesday after lunch. I joined in September because I enjoyed singing at home. At the first meeting, I knew nobody except a girl from my maths class, so I sat beside her.

The teacher gave each of us two ____2____ (song) to practise. One was slow and the other was cheerful. I put the pages in a folder so they would not disappear ____3____ my school bag among loose homework sheets.

Before our first concert, we practised standing in two rows. I was shorter than most of the others, so the teacher asked ____4____ (I) to stand at the front. That made me nervous because there would be nobody in front of me to follow.

My friend told me ____5____ (look) at the conductor, not at her. The conductor's hands would help everyone begin together. I watched ____6____ (careful) as the teacher showed us how a small movement could signal a quiet ending.

On the concert day, I wore ____7____ white shirt and dark trousers. My parents arrived early, but I could not see them clearly from the stage. The lights above us were ____8____ (bright) than the lights over the seats.

When the music began, I forgot to search for familiar faces. I listened to the voices beside me and sang with them. After ____9____ (finish), we waited for the conductor to lower her hands. Only then did we turn ____10____ the audience and smile. My parents said they had heard me. I liked knowing that my voice had also belonged to a much larger sound.

A birthday card for the rabbit

My little brother ____1____ (love) our pet rabbit, Snow. He says Snow should have a birthday like everyone else in the family. We do not know the rabbit's real birthday, so we use the day she came to live with us.

This year, my brother made three little ____2____ (card). One was from him, one from me and one from our parents. I helped him write the names, but he drew all the pictures ____3____ himself. Each picture showed Snow eating or sleeping.

Mum reminded ____4____ (we) that a rabbit could not read a card. My brother said the pictures were for Snow and the words were for us. He put the cards on a shelf outside her enclosure, where she could not chew them.

We decided ____5____ (spend) some time making her play area interesting. Mum checked the materials and helped us arrange a cardboard tunnel. Snow moved through it ____6____ (slow), stopping at the far end to look around.

My brother wanted to give her ____7____ enormous piece of birthday cake. Mum explained that human cake was not suitable rabbit food. We kept her ordinary feeding routine and enjoyed the cake ourselves instead.

The tunnel was ____8____ (long) than the old one. Before ____9____ (leave) Snow to explore, we made sure she could move through and out comfortably. My brother sat quietly nearby rather than lifting her into it. He was pleased when she chose to enter again.

At the end of the day, the cards were still ____10____ the shelf. Snow had not read a word, but my brother had spent a happy afternoon thinking about what she actually liked. That seemed a good way to mark her special day.

After ____7____ (practise) near the side, I moved a short distance towards the middle with the instructor's guidance. My arms ____8____ (hold) out for balance. I was not graceful, but I was no longer using the wall as a handle.

I noticed an animal ____2____ I could not name. It had a long nose and a heavy-looking body. My uncle did not ask me to guess forever. He showed me where the country's name was printed and suggested ____3____ (look) for reliable information about its wildlife.

My uncle asked me to handle the album ____5____ (careful). Some pages had old paper that could tear. We looked at the stamp without peeling it from its place, and he used a pointer rather than pressing a finger onto its surface.

Before ____8____ (leave), I chose one modern spare stamp to start a small page of my own. It was ____9____ ordinary stamp, not a rare or valuable one. The forecast before the match

Our school football match ____1____ (postpone) after heavy rain made the field unsuitable for play. I had seen a forecast showing only a small chance of rain and felt annoyed. I thought the forecast had promised us a dry afternoon.

The geography teacher asked me ____2____ (read) the wording again. A probability was not a promise that an event could never happen. Even a low chance did not rule ____3____ rain on some occasions. The meaning was less simple than the picture of a small sun had suggested.

We compared several weather ____4____ (report), noting their locations and publication times. A forecast made earlier could differ from a later update. We also checked whether the area described was the whole district or the particular place where our school stood.

After ____5____ (discuss) the examples, I understood why a screenshot without a time could be misleading. The teacher explained the distinction ____6____ (patient), without suggesting that every forecast was equally useful or that prediction was pointless.

The rescheduled match was arranged ____7____ the following Wednesday. This time, I checked the latest information and listened to the school's decision about the field. A dry sky at one moment did not automatically make the ground suitable.

We brought ____8____ (we) equipment only after the teacher confirmed the plan. It was ____9____ sensible arrangement because the people responsible could assess conditions we could not judge from a symbol on a screen. I still wanted accurate forecasts, but I now checked ____10____ (exact) what they said before turning them into a guarantee about my own afternoon.
